Senses.Explanation: Something described this way is perfectly round on every side, with no edge, corner, or seam. The expression occurs 132 times in 81 allowlisted texts. Hongzhi Zhengjue supplies the clearest physical constraint by saying that it is perfectly round and has no edges or corners. Shuzhong Wuyun applies the description to a begging bowl, calling it round and shining before describing where he throws or stores it. Yinyuan Longqi makes the same shape mobile by comparing it to a pearl running on a tray and a tray moving under the pearl; he then calls it perfectly round and lively, emerging and disappearing and opening and folding. In a separate three-part exchange, Yinyuan answers “what is buddha?” with “perfectly round,” “what is the teaching?” with “lively and active,” and “what is the monastic community?” with “freely at ease.” Zen bends a visible round, cornerless form into public answers and paired descriptive formulas, but the headword itself does not name one hidden substance, attainment, or universal abstract meaning.
Senses.Note: Other predicates retain the same rounded form while attaching different claims to it. Qianyan Yuanzhang pairs “perfectly round” with “shining and flashing,” then says “large within large, narrow within narrow.” Hongzhi Zhengjue says that the form is neither the least bit deficient nor the least bit excessive. Chunan Furong Baining Yi also criticizes a fixed reading: he says later people take “the perfectly round and shining one” as the ultimate rule, yet do not know that the Way has no fixed body and that heading toward it goes astray. His warning prevents the dictionary from converting a recurrent description into one universal abstract definition. The adverbial form occurs 15 times in 11 texts, and the exact round-and-shining pairing occurs three times in three texts.

Occurrences.Kwic: 傳家清白有風規。圓陀陀地無稜角。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Extensive Record of Chan Master Hongzhi (宏智禪師廣錄): Hongzhi Zhengjue's verse says the inherited family is clean and white with its established style, round and rolling, without edges or corners.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「如何是佛？」師云：「圓陀陀。」「如何是法？」師云：「活潑潑。」「如何是僧？」師云：「任騰騰。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yinyuan (隱元禪師語錄), Yinyuan Longqi's Huangbo Mountain record: asked what buddha is, Yinyuan Longqi answers 'perfectly round'; he answers the questions about the teaching and the monastic community with 'lively and active' and 'freely at ease.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 如盤走珠，如珠走盤，圓陀陀、活潑潑，出沒舒卷，無可不可。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yinyuan (隱元禪師語錄), Yinyuan Longqi's Huangbo Mountain record. In his Buddha-awakening-day hall address, Yinyuan Longqi compares a pearl moving on a tray and a tray moving under a pearl, then calls the movement perfectly round and lively, appearing and disappearing without obstruction.

Occurrences.Kwic: 致令後人認著個圓陀陀、光爍爍的以為極則，而殊不知道無體性，趣向則乖
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Complete Book of the Five Lamps, volumes 34–120 (五燈全書(第34卷-第120卷)), explicitly headed Chunan Furong Baining Yi: Chunan Furong Baining Yi says that later people take the perfectly round and shining description as the ultimate rule, yet do not know that the Way has no fixed body and that heading toward it goes astray.

Occurrences.Kwic: 處世界，無所著，圓陀陀，光爍爍，大中大，窄中窄。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Collected Guidelines of the Lineage Masters (列祖提綱錄), in Qianyan Yuanzhang's new-monks'-hall address: Qianyan Yuanzhang's verse pairs 'perfectly round' with 'shining and flashing,' then says 'large within large, narrow within narrow.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 圓陀陀地。曾無一毫頭許欠少。曾無一毫頭許盈餘。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Extensive Record of Chan Master Hongzhi (宏智禪師廣錄), in Hongzhi Zhengjue's discourse: Hongzhi Zhengjue predicates the round-and-rolling form as lacking not the least bit and having not the least bit in excess.

Occurrences.Kwic: 非銅非鐵亦非金，絕類離倫最奇絕。不徣借，不洗刮，圓陀陀兮光爍爍。有時擲向十字街頭，渾弗愛惜。有時收向百衲袋中，重重包括。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shuzhong Wuyun (恕中無慍禪師語錄), begging-bowl song written by Shuzhong Wuyun for monk Yuanshu: Shuzhong Wuyun calls the bowl round and shining, then describes throwing it into the crossroads or storing it in the patched-robe bag.

RelatedTerms: pearl running on a tray (盤走珠)
